# Cogeneration and On-Site Power {#sec-cogen}

## Cogeneration

Cogeneration, also called combined heat and power (CHP), makes useful heat and electricity in one system. An ordinary power plant throws away most of the heat from the fuel it burns; a CHP unit captures that heat and puts it to work, so far more of the fuel's energy ends up being used [@ricardo-aea_2013_001].

A CHP system has a *prime mover*, the engine that turns fuel into motion: a steam turbine, gas turbine, reciprocating engine, microturbine, or fuel cell. The prime mover drives a generator, and a heat-recovery unit captures the heat it gives off. CHP systems are named after their prime mover [@epa-2007]. They can burn biomass, biogas, natural gas, or coal, and the heat they recover can raise steam, heat water or air for drying, or drive absorption chillers for cooling.

Canadian industry already runs biomass CHP in pulp and paper, chemicals, wood products, and food processing. A typical plant burns biomass in a boiler whose steam drives a turbine; the steam that leaves the turbine, or steam drawn off partway through it, then serves the process. Using that heat can raise a plant's overall efficiency by more than 35 % [@epa-2007].

### How CIMS represents cogeneration

CIMS doesn't treat cogeneration as a service of its own. A CHP unit is one of the technologies that can supply a sector's **steam** service (see @sec-industrial-heat). The heat is what it provides, and the electricity is a by-product that reduces the electricity the site buys. This puts CHP in direct competition with boilers, heat pumps, and the other heat-supply technologies, on the full lifetime cost of meeting the site's steam demand.

The CHP technologies that compete in the steam services are:

- gas-turbine CHP, simple or combined cycle, where the turbine's hot exhaust raises process steam in a heat-recovery steam generator;
- reciprocating engine CHP, which recovers heat from the engine's cooling water and exhaust;
- back-pressure or extraction steam-turbine CHP, usually behind a fuel-fired or biomass boiler;
- fuel-cell CHP;
- biomass gasifier CHP, which turns biomass into a fuel gas for an engine or turbine; and
- gas-turbine or engine CHP with carbon capture on its exhaust.

Their descriptions and types are in the steam technology table in @sec-industrial-heat.

## On-site power generation

Some sites make electricity with no useful heat recovered. Off-grid mines and oil and gas sites run diesel and gas generators; other sites run gas turbines and engines, condensing steam turbines, or power plants that burn by-product gases; and remote operations increasingly add solar panels, wind turbines, and batteries in small local grids. At isolated northern mines, diesel can supply more than 80 % of all the energy used on site.

The line between cogeneration and on-site power is heat recovery. A unit that supplies useful heat competes in the steam service; one that doesn't competes for on-site power. One option sits on the line: a waste-heat power unit takes heat that a process would otherwise throw away and turns it into electricity, using an organic Rankine cycle or a steam turbine [@epa_2022_001; @hedman_2008_001].

Mining is the only sector with an **on-site power** service so far. Waste-heat power and other power-only options could serve other sectors, including cement, iron and steel, glass, refining, chemicals, pulp and paper, metal smelting, and offshore oil platforms, but those sectors don't have an on-site power service yet.
